paragraphs.heading: Mineral versus rock
paragraphs.text: Broadly speaking, a mineral is a solid substance that occurs naturally in pure form. Its chemical composition is fairly well defined, and it has a specific crystal structure. A rock is a different idea. A rock is any bulk solid geologic material that is fairly uniform at a large enough scale. It may be made of a single type of mineral, or it may be a mixture of two or more types.

paragraphs.heading: Tests a mineral must pass
paragraphs.text: Several requirements have to be met. A mineral must occur naturally and be formed by natural geological processes, whether on Earth or on other bodies beyond it. It must be a solid in its natural occurrence. It must have an ordered arrangement of atoms. And its chemical composition must be fairly well defined. The first test rules out compounds made directly and only by human activity or inside living beings, such as tungsten carbide and seashells.

paragraphs.heading: Same compound, different minerals
paragraphs.text: When one chemical compound occurs in nature with different crystal structures, each structure counts as a separate mineral species. Quartz and stishovite are an example: both consist of silicon dioxide, yet they are two different minerals. Some natural solids have no definite crystal structure at all. Opal and obsidian are like this, and they are more properly called mineraloids.

paragraphs.heading: Odd cases at the edges
paragraphs.text: Water and carbon dioxide are not considered minerals, but water ice is. A major exception to the solid rule is native mercury. It crystallizes only below −39 °C, yet the International Mineralogical Association (IMA) still classifies it as a mineral because it was included before the present rules were set. Some authors require a solid that is stable or metastable at room temperature (25 °C). The IMA asks only for enough stability that the structure and composition of the substance can be well determined. It recognizes meridianiite, a natural hydrate of magnesium sulfate, even though that mineral forms and stays stable only below 2 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Describing and sorting minerals
paragraphs.text: Besides its chemistry and crystal structure, the description of a mineral usually lists common physical properties such as hardness, lustre, colour, streak and cleavage. Minerals are classified by their key chemical ingredients, and the two dominant systems are the Dana and the Strunz classifications. Silicate minerals make up about 90% of Earth's crust. Other important groups include the native elements, each made of a single pure element, along with sulfides such as galena (PbS), halides such as rock salt (NaCl) and carbonates such as calcite (CaCO₃).

paragraphs.heading: Who decides, and how names work
paragraphs.text: The IMA is the generally recognized body that sets the definitions and names of mineral species. As of August 2026 it lists more than 6,200 of them. Minerals are most often named after a person, and the next most common source is the place of discovery. Most names end in "-ite". The exceptions, such as galena and diamond, are usually names that were well established before mineralogy was organized as a discipline.

paragraphs.heading: The argument over living things
paragraphs.text: The geological definition normally leaves out compounds that occur only in living organisms. However, some minerals, calcite among them, are often biogenic, meaning produced in living beings. Living organisms also often make inorganic minerals that occur in rocks too, hydroxylapatite being one. The IMA's choice to exclude crystalline substances made by living things has been a point of contention among geologists and mineralogists. One author, Skinner (2005), views all solids as potential minerals and counts biominerals, the ones created by the metabolic activity of organisms, as part of the mineral kingdom.
